slides.title: Deception Technology
slides.teach: Deception technology uses fake resources to trick attackers into interacting with something that appears real.

course.learn: Deception technology uses fake resources to trick attackers into interacting with something that appears real.
course.why: Legitimate users usually have no reason to interact with decoys, so interaction can be a strong sign of suspicious activity.
course.example: A fake server is intentionally deployed so defenders can observe attackers who interact with it.
course.check_q: A fake server is created to attract attackers. What security approach is this?

slides.title: Disruption Technology
slides.teach: Disruption technology uses security techniques to interfere with, redirect, isolate, or slow down an attack.

course.learn: Disruption technology uses security techniques to interfere with, redirect, isolate, or slow down an attack.

breakdown.explanation: Interrupt what the attacker is trying to accomplish.
Redirecting malicious traffic, isolating compromised systems, and sending attackers toward decoys.

course.why: Disruption reduces an attacker's ability to communicate, move, or complete an attack.
course.example: Malware traffic is redirected away from its intended malicious destination.
course.check_q: A defender redirects malicious traffic to prevent the attacker from reaching the intended destination. Which concept applies?

slides.title: Honeypot
slides.teach: A honeypot is a fake system or service designed to attract attackers.

course.learn: A honeypot is a fake system or service designed to attract attackers.

breakdown.explanation: It is believable bait that gives defenders a place to observe suspicious behavior without exposing a real production system.
A decoy server, fake SSH service, or intentionally vulnerable-looking host.

course.why: Legitimate users normally have no reason to attack the decoy, so interaction can be a strong sign of malicious activity.
course.example: A company deploys a fake server that appears vulnerable so the SOC can observe attackers who interact with it.
course.check_q: A decoy server is deployed to attract and observe attackers. What is it?

slides.title: Honeynet
slides.teach: A honeynet is a fake network containing multiple decoy systems.

course.learn: A honeynet is a fake network containing multiple decoy systems.

breakdown.explanation: Instead of one fake host, defenders create an entire believable decoy environment.
Multiple honeypots, a decoy subnet, or a fake enterprise environment.

course.why: A honeynet can reveal how an attacker moves between systems and attempts lateral movement.
course.example: An attacker enters a decoy subnet containing several fake servers while defenders observe the attack path.
course.check_q: A decoy environment contains multiple fake systems. What is it?

slides.title: Honeyfile
slides.teach: A honeyfile is a fake file designed to look valuable so unauthorized access can reveal suspicious activity.

course.learn: A honeyfile is a fake file designed to look valuable so unauthorized access can reveal suspicious activity.

breakdown.explanation: It is a file-shaped trap: normal users should have little or no reason to open it.
Fake payroll files, fake customer lists, or fake confidential documents.

course.why: Opening or copying a honeyfile can trigger an alert and reveal unauthorized browsing or data theft.
course.example: A file named Executive_Payroll_CONFIDENTIAL.xlsx triggers an alert when an unauthorized user opens it.
course.check_q: A tempting fake document is used to detect unauthorized access. What is it?

slides.title: Honeytoken
slides.teach: A honeytoken is fake data or a fake credential that should never be legitimately used.

course.learn: A honeytoken is fake data or a fake credential that should never be legitimately used.

breakdown.explanation: If the fake value is used, defenders know something suspicious probably happened.
A fake API key, password, account, access token, or database record.

course.why: Honeytokens are useful because legitimate activity should never require the planted value.
course.example: A fake API key is planted in a repository and generates an alert if anyone attempts to use it.
course.check_q: A planted fake API key generates an alert when used. What is it?

cards.name: Deception Technology

blocks.title: Know all four honey technologies
blocks.prompt: What kind of fake resource is being used?

cards.name: Honeypot
cards.definition: A fake system or service designed to attract attackers so defenders can detect and observe suspicious activity.

cards.name: Honeynet
cards.definition: A fake network made of multiple decoy systems so defenders can observe attacker movement.

cards.name: Honeyfile
cards.definition: A fake file designed to look valuable so unauthorized access can reveal suspicious activity.

cards.name: Honeytoken
cards.definition: Fake data or credentials that should never be used legitimately; use can trigger an alert.

blocks.title: Deception technology quick reference
rows: Attracts attackers to a decoy so their behavior can be observed
Creates a decoy environment with multiple systems
Looks valuable and reveals suspicious access
Triggers detection if fake credentials, keys, accounts, or records are used

blocks.title: Deception = trick · Disruption = interrupt
items: Deception technology uses fake resources that look real so attackers interact with them instead of legitimate assets.
Example: A fake server is deployed to attract attackers and let defenders observe them.
A honeypot is one fake system or service.
Example: A decoy SSH server attracts brute-force attempts.
A honeynet is a fake network containing multiple decoy systems.
Example: A decoy subnet lets defenders observe attacker lateral movement.
Honeyfile → fake FILE · Honeytoken → fake DATA/CREDENTIAL
A honeyfile is a fake document; a honeytoken is fake data or a fake credential that should never be legitimately used.
Example: A fake payroll spreadsheet is a honeyfile; a planted fake API key is a honeytoken.
Disruption interferes with, redirects, isolates, or slows an attack.
Example: Malicious traffic is redirected away from its intended destination.
blocks.example: Memory: Pot = system · Net = network · File = file · Token = data/credential.

questions.q: A fake server is deployed to attract and observe attackers. What is it?
questions.explanation: A honeypot is a decoy system or service designed to attract attackers.

questions.q: A fake network of multiple decoy systems is deployed to observe attacker movement. What is this?
questions.explanation: A honeynet is a decoy network containing multiple systems.

questions.q: A fake confidential spreadsheet triggers an alert when an unauthorized user opens it. What is it?
questions.explanation: A honeyfile is a fake file designed to reveal suspicious access.

questions.q: A fake API key is planted where an attacker may find it and generates an alert if used. What is this?
questions.explanation: A honeytoken is fake data or a fake credential that should never be legitimately used.

questions.q: Malicious traffic is redirected away from its intended destination to interfere with an attack. Which concept applies?
questions.explanation: Disruption technology interferes with or redirects an attack.

questions.q: Which phrase BEST distinguishes deception from disruption?
questions.explanation: Deception uses bait or fake resources, while disruption interferes with attacker activity.
